# MDR Software Classification: tablet control app for [X] infusion pump

**Intended purpose (as stated):** "to set and adjust the delivery rate of the [X] infusion pump under clinician control."
**Qualified as a device:** assumed established — see note in Limits

## Class: III

**Route:** 3.3 → same class as the driven device (the [X] infusion pump, Class III). **Rule 11 is never reached.**

## Reasoning

| Step | Question | Answer | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | Intended purpose | "to set and adjust the delivery rate of the [X] infusion pump under clinician control" | `[verified]` |
| 3.3 | Drives or influences another device? | **Yes** — it sets the pump's delivery rate. This is driving, not displaying. | `[verified]` |
| 3.3 | Consequence | Falls within the same class as that device → the pump's class governs → **III** | `[verified]` |
| Rule 11 | Which limb | **Not reached.** 3.3 applies before Rule 11; Rule 11 governs only software independent of any other device. | `[verified]` |
| Rule 11 | Escalation | N/A | `[verified]` |
| 3.5 | Could a stricter rule apply? | **No practical effect** — III is the highest class, so no stricter rule can raise it. | `[verified]` |

The "it doesn't diagnose anything" point is the thing to set aside deliberately. It is a correct observation and it is not the question 3.3 asks. Rule 11's diagnostic and monitoring limbs — the limbs where "no diagnostic function" would matter — are only in play for software that is *independent of any other device*. Yours sets an operating parameter on a specific pump, so it is classified by the pump, not by what it does or doesn't infer. Displaying the current rate would, on its own, likely be independent-and-displaying; but the setting function dominates and is squarely within the stated intended purpose.

## What would change this

- **The pump's class.** The whole answer is inherited. If the [X] pump were Class IIb, the app would be IIb.
- **Removing the setting function.** A build that only *displays* the current rate, with no ability to set or adjust and no gating of alarms, would plausibly be independent software and would then go to Rule 11 — where a pure-display readout with no diagnostic or monitoring purpose lands in limb 3, class I. That is a different product, not a different reading of this one.
- **Whether the app is placed on the market as its own product or as a part of the pump.** If it is a component of the pump system rather than a separately-supplied product, the question is not "what class is the app" but "the app is part of the pump's Class III technical documentation." Either way the rigour is Class III; what changes is whether you hold a separate classification, UDI and declaration for it. Worth pinning down explicitly, because it drives your documentation structure. `[verify]` — this turns on Art. 2(1) and placing-on-the-market concepts I don't carry here.
- **Capability beyond the stated purpose.** If the app can do more than set/adjust/display — compute a dose from patient weight, suggest a rate, warn on an interaction — that doesn't raise the class above III, but it does mean the intended purpose as written may be understating the product. Flagging as a note, not a classification finding.

## Limits

> This classifies software under MDR Annex VIII implementing rules 3.1–3.7 and Rule 11, retrieved verbatim from EUR-Lex on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover Art. 2(1) qualification, Rules 1–10 or 12–22, Annex XVI, IVDR, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, or national interpretation. Rule 11 is a floor: under 3.5 a stricter rule this skill does not carry may raise the class. A structured first pass and an audit aid, not legal or regulatory advice, and not a substitute for your notified body or a qualified regulatory professional.

Nothing you've given me settles Art. 2(1) qualification — I've assumed it, which is safe here since software driving a Class III pump is not a borderline qualification case, but it is formally a separate analysis.

## Before you build on this

This is the Annex VIII text applied to the intended purpose as you stated it. The class drives your conformity route, whether you need a notified body, and the depth of your technical documentation, so it should be confirmed by your regulatory lead or notified body before you build on it. The three things to put in front of them:

1. **The 3.3 call** — that setting the delivery rate is "driving" the pump, so the app inherits Class III rather than being classified in its own right.
2. **That Rule 11 is not reached at all** — so the absence of a diagnostic function is not a route to a lower class.
3. **Product-boundary question** — separate product inheriting III, or a part of the pump covered by the pump's own documentation. Not a class question, but it determines what artefacts you owe.

graders.evidence:
## Class III

Under EU MDR 2017/745, the governing text isn't Rule 11 — it's the implementing rule in **Annex VIII, Section 3.3**:

> "Software, which drives a device or influences the use of a device, shall fall within the same class as the device. If the software is independent of any other device, it shall be classified in its own right."

Your app drives the pump (it sets the delivery rate) and is not independent of it. So it inherits the pump's class: **III**.

### Why the "it doesn't diagnose anything" reasoning doesn't help

Rule 11 is the classification rule for *independent* MDSW — software that provides information used for diagnostic or therapeutic decisions. That's the rule people reach for, and it's the wrong one here. Yours isn't information-providing software that a clinician reads and acts on; it's the control interface that actuates the pump. Section 3.3 is applied before you ever get to Rule 11, and 3.3 doesn't care about diagnosis. Nor does "under clinician control" reduce the class — the clinician setting a value in your UI is exactly the "drives the device" scenario, not an exemption from it. MDCG 2019-11 (qualification and classification of MDSW) is consistent on both points.

### The one question that actually changes your answer

Not the class — that's III either way — but the regulatory *route*:

- **Part of the pump** (placed on the market as a component of the device, same technical documentation, same certificate, same UDI-DI family): most likely, if the app is the only way to set the rate. The pump's existing Class III certificate covers it; you're managing a change to an existing device, not certifying a new one.
- **Accessory** (separately CE-marked, e.g. sold standalone, or works across a product line you didn't originally certify together): accessories are classified in their own right (Annex VIII 3.2), but 3.3 still lands you on Class III — now with its own technical documentation, own Annex IX assessment, own UDI.

Worth settling explicitly with your notified body, because the second path is substantially more work than most teams expect.

### Practical consequences of Class III

- Annex IX conformity assessment: full QMS audit **plus** technical documentation assessment of the specific device by the notified body (no self-certification, no sampling relief).
- **IEC 62304 software safety class C** — an incorrect or unintended infusion rate can cause death or serious injury. Full architectural design, detailed design, unit verification, and SOUP documentation for the tablet OS and every third-party library.
- Clinical evaluation with data (Article 61 — Class III implantables aside, expectations are high), plus PMCF.
- Article 54 scrutiny doesn't apply (that's Class III implantables), but expect heavy scrutiny anyway.

### Things I'd flag now, before the class debate is even resolved

- **General-purpose tablet as the platform.** You need to bound the computing platform in your technical documentation — OS versions, hardware, what happens on OS auto-update, what happens if another app steals focus or the battery dies mid-titration. This is usually the hardest part of a tablet-based pump controller.
- **Cybersecurity** — MDCG 2019-16, and the interface between tablet and pump is now a safety-critical channel.
- **IEC 62366-1 usability engineering** — for a Class III rate-setting UI, a summative validation study is effectively mandatory.
- **Alarms** — if the app displays or relays any alarm condition, IEC 60601-1-8 comes into scope, and alarm reliability on a consumer tablet is a genuinely hard problem.
- **Risk control allocation.** If the pump itself enforces hard rate limits independently of the app, say so prominently in your risk file; it doesn't lower the class, but it materially changes the risk argument.

I'm giving you the reasoning from the regulation text, not a regulatory sign-off — get your RA lead or notified body to confirm the part-of-device vs. accessory call in writing, since that one determines your submission structure.

## Short answer: Class III

Not via Rule 11 — via the implementing rule.

**MDR Annex VIII, Chapter II, Rule 3.3:**
> "Software, which drives a device or influences the use of a device, shall fall within the same class as the device. If the software is independent of any other device, it shall be classified in its own right."

Your app sets the infusion rate. That is *driving* the pump in the most literal sense — it commands the therapy-delivering actuator. So it inherits the pump's class: **III**.

Rule 11 doesn't apply here. Rule 11 is for software that's independent of another device and provides information for diagnostic/therapeutic decisions. Yours isn't providing information for a clinician to act on; it *is* the control path. (Even if you forced Rule 11, "could cause death or irreversible deterioration" would land you at III anyway — so there's no cheaper reading.)

The "it doesn't diagnose anything" argument doesn't help. Diagnosis is only one route to a high class; control of a hazardous therapy is another.

## The question that actually matters more

**Is this a separate device, or part of the pump?** This has bigger practical consequences than the class, and MDCG 2019-11 is the guidance to read.

- **Part of the pump** (same manufacturer, placed on the market as one system, covered by the pump's technical documentation, clinical evaluation, and CE certificate): no separate CE mark, no separate UDI-DI for the app, no second conformity assessment. Given it's *your* pump, this is usually the right and much lighter path.
- **Accessory placed on the market separately**: classified in its own right (Art. 51(1)) — still Class III by Rule 3.3 — with its own tech doc, UDI, declaration of conformity, and notified body route.

If the app ships only with your pump and is versioned with it, argue for "part of the device." If you sell/distribute it independently (app store, works across pump models, separate release cadence), a notified body will likely push you to accessory.

## Consequences either way

- **Conformity assessment**: Annex IX (QMS + technical documentation assessment) — notified body involved, no self-certification. Art. 54 clinical evaluation consultation targets Class III *implantable* devices, so it shouldn't catch you, but confirm with your NB.
- **IEC 62304 safety class C.** Separate axis from MDR class, but a wrong rate on a Class III pump means death or serious injury, and no external risk control fully mitigates it from the software's side. Full architecture, detailed design, unit verification, and SOUP requirements apply.
- **The tablet is part of your risk story.** General-purpose OS, other apps, screen failures, touch misregistration, backgrounding, battery death mid-titration, OS auto-updates. You must specify minimum host requirements and treat the platform as SOUP-adjacent. IEC 62366-1 usability engineering will be heavily scrutinized on rate entry — decimal point errors, unit confusion, confirmation steps.
- **Displaying the current rate is a safety function**, not a convenience. If the app shows a stale or wrong rate, the clinician acts on it. Treat display integrity, staleness detection, and connection-loss behavior as risk controls with real requirements.
- **Pump-side independent limits.** Your best architectural lever: the pump enforces its own hard rate bounds and validates commands, so the app can't command an unsafe rate even if it misbehaves. Doesn't lower the MDR class, but it substantially improves the risk file and the 62304 argument.

One caveat: I'm reasoning from the MDR text and MDCG guidance, not giving regulatory advice. The part-of-device vs. accessory call in particular should be agreed with your notified body in writing before you build the technical documentation around it.

The relevant provision isn't Rule 11. It's **Annex VIII, Chapter II (Implementing Rules), point 3.3** of MDR 2017/745:

> "Software, which drives a device or influences the use of a device, shall fall within the same class as the device. If the software is independent of any other device, it shall be classified in its own right."

The fact that it doesn't diagnose is irrelevant here. That reasoning would matter under Rule 11 (which classifies on the basis of information provided for diagnostic/therapeutic decisions), but Rule 11 only comes into play for software that's independent of any other device. Yours isn't. And per implementing rule 3.5, if you did try to apply both, the stricter result governs anyway.

MDCG 2019-11 confirms this reading: software driving or influencing a hardware device takes that device's class, and isn't classified as standalone MDSW.

## Two things worth pinning down

**1. Is this a separate device, or part of the pump?** The class is III either way, but the route differs:

- **Component of the pump system** (same manufacturer, placed on the market as part of the pump): it lives inside the pump's existing technical documentation and Class III certificate. No separate CE marking or Basic UDI-DI. This is usually the cleaner path since you make both.
- **Placed on the market separately** (e.g. an app store download, or sold as an add-on): it needs its own CE marking, own Basic UDI-DI, own conformity assessment — as a Class III device, meaning Annex IX full QMS *plus* technical documentation assessment by your notified body.

If you're currently treating it as a loosely-coupled app but shipping it with the pump, decide this deliberately and document it — notified bodies push on exactly this point.

**2. Sanity-check the pump's own class.** Infusion pumps are typically **Class IIb** under Rule 12 (devices administering medicinal products), escalating to III only in specific circumstances — e.g. implantable (Rule 8) or where the mode of administration is potentially hazardous given the substance and body part. If the pump is genuinely III, fine, the app is III. But if someone assigned III conservatively without working the rule, you're voluntarily taking on a much heavier assessment burden for the whole product line. Worth confirming against the pump's actual classification rationale.

- IEC 62304 software safety **Class C** almost certainly (an erroneous rate can cause death or serious injury) — full architectural design, detailed design, and unit verification records.
- Notified body scrutiny of the technical documentation, not just QMS sampling.
- Annex I §17 applies in full: software lifecycle, repeatability/reliability, and — because it's a tablet — §17.3/17.4 obligations to specify the minimum hardware, IT characteristics, and IT security measures for the computing platform. Off-the-shelf tablet hardware needs an explicit spec and a story about what happens on unqualified devices.
- Cybersecurity per MDCG 2019-16, and the wireless link between tablet and pump is a hazard source in its own right (loss of connection mid-titration, command corruption, unauthorised commands, latency between input and confirmation).
- Usability engineering per IEC 62366-1 — the rate-entry UI is a use-error hotspot (decimal placement, unit confusion, unintended repeat).
- PMS plan, PSUR, and trend reporting on the Class III cadence (PSUR annually).

## Bottom line

**Class III, MDR Annex VIII, Rule 11, first indent.**

## Qualification first

- **It's software, and it's MDSW.** It performs an action on data beyond storage, archiving, communication or simple search — it interprets CTA images and produces a patient-specific finding. That satisfies Art. 2(1) ("diagnosis, prediction, prognosis... of disease") and MDCG 2019-11's qualification steps.
- **MDR, not IVDR.** Input is imaging data, not data derived from a specimen from the human body, so Rule 11 of MDR Annex VIII applies, not IVDR Annex VIII Rule 3.
- **Classified in its own right.** Since it's standalone and not driving or influencing another device, Annex VIII implementing rule 3.3 means it does not inherit the class of the CT scanner — it gets its own classification.

## Why Rule 11 first indent

Rule 11's opening paragraph: software intended to provide information used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes is **class IIa**, *except* where those decisions have an impact that may cause:

- death or irreversible deterioration → **class III**
- serious deterioration or a surgical intervention → **class IIb**

Your stated intended purpose puts you squarely in the opening paragraph — the output *is* information used to take a therapeutic decision. The only question is which exception bites.

Both do, and rule 3.5 (highest applicable class) resolves it upward:

- Mechanical thrombectomy is a **surgical intervention** → IIb floor.
- A **false negative** means an LVO patient is not taken for thrombectomy inside the treatment window. The consequence is established infarct: severe irreversible neurological deficit or death. A **false positive** sends a patient to an invasive intra-arterial procedure with real risk of vessel injury, symptomatic haemorrhage and death.

Either error pathway meets "impact that may cause death or an irreversible deterioration of a person's state of health." → **Class III.**

The IMDRF framing that MDCG 2019-11 §5.3 imports agrees: significance of information = *drives clinical management* (arguably *treat/diagnose*), healthcare situation = *critical*. That is the top cell of the matrix.

## The IIb argument, and why I wouldn't rely on it

The usual manufacturer position is: it's only *triage*, the neurointerventionalist reads the CTA themselves, so the human in the loop catches any error, and the surgical-intervention indent (IIb) is the right one.

Two problems:

1. **Rule 11 contains no human-in-the-loop exemption.** That concept comes from FDA's clinical decision support thinking (and the "independently review the basis" carve-out in the 21st Century Cures Act), not from MDR. Importing it is a common and expensive mistake.
2. Your own intended purpose says the output is used *to decide whether to take the patient straight to thrombectomy*. That describes bypassing or compressing the independent read, which is the whole clinical value proposition. You can't claim the time saving in your clinical evidence and the independent review in your classification rationale.

If you genuinely want to argue IIb, the intended purpose has to be rewritten so the software is a prioritisation/notification aid that does not inform the treat/no-treat decision — and then your clinical claims and labelling have to live inside that narrower box. That's a commercial decision, not a regulatory workaround, and I'd expect a notified body to push back hard on it for an LVO indication. Market precedent in this space is genuinely mixed, so whichever way you go, write a documented classification rationale against Rule 11's wording and get it in front of your NB early rather than at submission.

## What Class III actually costs you

- Conformity assessment via **Annex IX** (full QMS + technical documentation assessment for the device) or Annex X + XI. Notified body mandatory either way.
- **Art. 61(4): clinical investigations are required** for class III devices, unless you can rely on equivalence to a device you already market, or on existing clinical data with a justification the NB accepts. This is usually the schedule-driving item — plan for a prospective study.
- **SSCP** under Art. 32, validated by the NB and published in Eudamed.
- **Annual PSUR**, updated PMCF, Art. 10(14) obligations, UDI/Eudamed registration.
- Class III carries **NB scrutiny/expert panel consultation** exposure under Art. 54 only for implantables/class IIb administering medicines, so that one doesn't apply here.
- Note that the Art. 120 transitional extensions (31 Dec 2027 for class III) are only available with a valid legacy MDD certificate plus an NB application lodged by 26 May 2024 and a signed agreement by 26 Sep 2024. Those gates have closed — so if this is a new device or was MDD class I self-certified, you're on the full MDR route now.

## Assumptions I've made

EU MDR 2017/745 (not UKCA — MHRA is still on UK MDR 2002, where this would be class IIa under the old MDD Rule 10/12 logic, pending the new UK framework). I've also assumed no closed-loop action, no dosing output, and no paediatric or emergency-service-dispatch use, any of which would need a fresh look.

## Qualification first

It's medical device software in its own right (MDSW under MDCG 2019-11): it processes patient images and creates new medical information for an individual patient, for a diagnostic/therapeutic purpose. Article 2(1) MDR is satisfied.

Because it's standalone and doesn't drive or influence another device, Annex VIII Implementing Rule 3.3 sends you to classify it on its own — not in the class of the CT scanner.

## Applicable rule: Rule 11, first indent

> "Software intended to provide information which is used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes is classified as class IIa, except if such decisions have an impact that may cause: death or an irreversible deterioration of a person's state of health, in which case it is in class III..."

**Classification: Class III.**

Your intended purpose says the output supports the decision to proceed to mechanical thrombectomy. Run both error directions:

- **False negative** — LVO not flagged, thrombectomy not performed or delayed. In acute ischaemic stroke this is irreversible infarction of salvageable tissue, up to death. First indent, Class III.
- **False positive** — patient taken to an unnecessary endovascular procedure carrying vessel perforation, dissection and haemorrhage risk. On its own that's at least "surgical intervention" → Class IIb, and arguably death/irreversible harm → III.

The worse branch governs, and Implementing Rule 3.5 confirms the strictest applicable rule wins. Class III.

## The arguments that don't get you down to IIb

Two are usually attempted, and neither works under MDR as written:

1. **"A neurointerventionalist reviews the images anyway — we're only decision support."** MDR Rule 11 has no human-in-the-loop carve-out. That concept comes from the US (21st Century Cures §520(o)(1)(E) and the FDA CDS guidance), and it does not transfer. MDCG 2019-11 asks about the significance of the information to the decision and the situation of the patient, not whether a clinician double-checks.
2. **"It's only triage."** Your own intended purpose defeats this: "to support the decision to proceed to mechanical thrombectomy." That's a therapeutic decision, stated by you, in a time-critical pathway where the whole point is to compress decision time. A notified body will read the intended purpose as written.

## Where the class could actually move

The lever is the intended purpose, not the algorithm. There is a genuine distinction between:

- **Decision-informing** (your current wording) → Class III; and
- **Pure workflow prioritisation / parallel notification** — the software reorders a worklist or pages the on-call team, explicitly does not provide diagnostic information, does not replace the radiologist's or interventionalist's independent review of the images, and the standard-of-care read happens regardless. This is the CADt-style framing, and it's a defensible route to IIa, sometimes IIb.

If you want that lower class you have to actually mean it, and it has to hold across labelling, UI, training material and your clinical evidence — the output cannot be presented as a finding, the human review must be a genuine independent step rather than a rubber stamp, and the claimed benefit must be time-to-notification rather than detection. Given "the output is used by the on-call neurointerventionalist to decide whether to take the patient straight to thrombectomy," you are not in that space today. I'd plan on Class III.

## Consequences worth pricing in

- Notified body conformity assessment via Annex IX (QMS + technical documentation assessment of every device) or Annex X + XI.
- Article 61(4): clinical investigation is the default for Class III; an equivalence or existing-data justification is possible but hard for a novel algorithm, and you'd need contractual access to the comparator's technical documentation.
- SSCP required, annual PSUR, PMCF plan, UDI, EUDAMED registration.
- Not subject to the Article 54 clinical evaluation consultation procedure — that's limited to Class III implantables and certain Class IIb active devices.
- Standards: IEC 62304, IEC 82304-1, ISO 14971, IEC 62366-1, plus GSPR 17.
- EU AI Act: as a device requiring third-party conformity assessment under MDR, this is high-risk under Article 6(1). Expect the AI Act requirements to be assessed through the same notified body, with the medical device track applying from August 2027.

Worth confirming the Rule 11 reasoning with your notified body early — the borderline between the two intended-purpose framings above is where they push back hardest, and it's much cheaper to settle before the technical documentation is written.

## Short answer

**Class III under Rule 11**, on the intended purpose as you've written it. Class IIb is arguable but, in my view, hard to defend against that specific wording.

## Working through it

**1. Qualification — is it a device?**

Yes. Article 2(1) covers software with a medical purpose including "diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, prediction, prognosis." Applying the MDCG 2019-11 decision steps: it performs an action on data beyond storage, archival, lossless compression or simple search, and it acts for the benefit of an individual patient. So it's Medical Device Software (MDSW). Not an IVD — it acts on images, not specimens.

**2. Standalone vs. accessory**

Annex VIII implementing rule 3.3: software that drives or influences a device takes that device's class; *software independent of any other device is classified in its own right*. You've said no connection to any other device, so it's classified on its own — you can't borrow the CT scanner's class.

**3. Rule 11**

The relevant limb:

> Software intended to provide information which is used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes is classified as class IIa, except if such decisions have an impact that may cause:
> — death or an irreversible deterioration of a person's state of health, in which case it is in class III; or
> — a serious deterioration of a person's state of health or a surgical intervention, in which case it is classified as class IIb.

Your baseline is IIa (information used for a therapeutic decision), then you test the escalations against the *decision*, not against the software:

- **False negative** — LVO not flagged, thrombectomy not performed or delayed. In an acute LVO the consequence is infarct progression: irreversible neurological deficit or death. That's the class III limb.
- **False positive** — patient taken to the angio suite unnecessarily: arterial puncture, contrast load, risk of dissection, perforation, haemorrhage. That is both "a surgical intervention" and plausibly "serious deterioration" — the IIb limb.

Implementing rule 3.5: where several sub-rules apply, the strictest applies. Both limbs are in play, so **Class III**.

## The counter-argument, and why I don't think it holds here

The IIb argument runs: the software is adjunctive, the neurointerventionalist independently reads the source CTA, and no decision is ever taken on the software output alone — so the software cannot itself cause irreversible harm.

Two problems:

1. Classification under Annex VIII is driven by **intended purpose**, not by residual risk after mitigation. Human-in-the-loop is a risk control, and risk controls don't downgrade a class. Notified bodies push back on this consistently.
2. Your own intended purpose statement ties the output directly to the treatment decision: *"to support the decision to proceed to mechanical thrombectomy."* That is a therapeutic decision whose failure mode is irreversible. You've written the class III escalation into the claim.

**This is the actual lever.** Some LVO triage products on the EU market sit at IIa/IIb — but look at how they're worded. They're typically framed as *notification and workflow prioritisation*: alerting a specialist that a study warrants earlier review, with explicit statements that the output is not diagnostic and does not replace review of the images. That intended purpose supports a lower class because the decision the information feeds is "which scan do I look at next," not "do I take this patient to the angio suite."

If your product genuinely only prioritises the worklist, reword the intended purpose to say so and IIb (arguably IIa) becomes defensible. If it genuinely informs the thrombectomy decision, keep the wording and accept III — Article 7 and the general obligation for the intended purpose to reflect actual clinical use mean you can't paper over the real use case. Also be aware that market precedent may be legacy MDD CE marks, where standalone software commonly sat in class I; Rule 11 exists precisely to end that.

## What Class III means for you practically

- **Conformity assessment:** Article 52(3) — Annex IX Chapters I and III plus technical documentation assessment under Chapter II, or Annex X type-examination plus Annex XI Part A. Notified body involvement either way; no self-certification.
- **No clinical evaluation consultation procedure.** Article 54 catches class III *implantable* devices and certain class IIb actives — standalone software isn't caught. Worth knowing, it removes one of the more painful class III steps.
- **Clinical data:** Article 61(4) — for class III devices, clinical investigations are expected unless you can justify reliance on equivalence, which requires contractual access to the other manufacturer's technical documentation. In practice, plan a clinical investigation.
- **SSCP** required (Article 32), annual **PSUR** (Article 86), PMCF plan, UDI and Eudamed registration, PRRC.
- **Standards:** IEC 62304 software safety class C, ISO 14971, IEC 82304-1, and — since it's presumably ML-based — IEC/AAMI 34971 and the usual expectations around dataset provenance, generalisability and off-distribution behaviour.
- **AI Act:** class III means notified body conformity assessment, so it's a high-risk AI system under Article 6(1) / Annex I. Article 8(2) lets you fold the AI Act requirements into a single MDR technical file and conformity assessment rather than running two parallel processes.

One planning note: the classification of your Class III determination will not shift, but the *evidence bar* differs sharply between "triage prioritisation" and "supports the thrombectomy decision" — the latter needs performance data at the operating point clinicians will actually act on, including false-negative rate stratified by occlusion site. Worth settling the intended purpose before you scope the clinical investigation, not after.

This is my reading of the regulation, not regulatory advice — get the intended purpose wording and the class agreed with your notified body early, because it determines your entire evidence and audit route.

## Bottom line

**Most likely Class IIa under MDR Annex VIII, Rule 11** — assuming it qualifies as a medical device at all. There is a real, but narrow, argument that it isn't a device. There is essentially no route to Class I here.

## Step 1: does it qualify? (MDCG 2019-11)

This is the decision that actually matters, and "trend" is the load-bearing word in your intended purpose.

Software is **not** MDSW if it only stores, archives, communicates, losslessly compresses, or does simple search on data. A pure logbook — the patient types 78.4 kg / 142/88, the app stores it, and later renders the stored values on a time axis — is arguably just display of stored data, i.e. not a device.

Software **is** MDSW if it performs an action on data beyond that, for the benefit of an individual patient, with one of the Article 2(1) purposes — and **monitoring** of a disease is explicitly one of them.

Where you fall depends on things not settled by your description:

- If "trend" means a chart of raw points → defensible non-device.
- If it computes anything — rolling/moving averages, rate of change, % change from baseline, "dry weight" deltas, regression lines, colour-coded ranges, out-of-range highlighting — that's an action on data, and combined with a CKD population it reads as monitoring. → MDSW.
- Your target population is the other problem. Weight + BP in *chronic kidney disease* patients, shown to a *nephrologist*, is not a wellness use case. Fluid status and BP control are the clinical variables in CKD management. A regulator will read the intended purpose in light of who it's for.

Note "no alarms / not for acute decisions" does **not** get you out of qualification. It only affects the class.

## Step 2: classification, if it's a device

Rule 11 has three limbs. Two could apply, both landing on IIa:

- **Decision-support limb** — "information used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes" → **IIa** by default. Escalates to IIb if such decisions may cause serious deterioration or surgical intervention, III if death or irreversible deterioration. Your facts argue against escalation: non-acute, clinician-mediated, reviewed at a scheduled appointment alongside labs and clinic BP.
- **Monitoring limb** — "monitoring of physiological processes" → **IIa**, escalating to IIb only for *vital* physiological parameters where variation could result in immediate danger. Blood pressure is a vital parameter, but once-daily home entry with no alarms and no acute use is the opposite of immediate danger. So IIa, not IIb.

The Rule 11 "all other software → Class I" catch-all is for software that neither drives a device nor provides information for decisions. A trending tool explicitly intended for review by a nephrologist doesn't fit that; if you can't reach Class I honestly, you're better off arguing non-qualification than arguing Class I.

## What IIa costs you

Notified body involvement (Annex IX Ch. I+III, or Annex XI), ISO 13485 QMS, IEC 62304 (likely software safety class A or B), IEC 82304-1, ISO 14971, usability per IEC 62366-1, clinical evaluation per Annex XIV and MDCG 2020-1, PMS/PMCF, UDI, and an EU-based manufacturer or authorised representative. No MDR Article 120 transitional relief — that only applies to legacy devices with a prior MDD certificate.

## Practical advice

1. **Decide deliberately whether the app computes anything**, and write that decision down. This single engineering choice moves you between "not a device" and "Class IIa." Don't let a developer add a 7-day moving average in a sprint and silently reclassify your product.
2. If you go the non-device route, produce a **written qualification rationale** against MDCG 2019-11 and keep it current — competent authorities will ask, and it needs to survive your own marketing copy. Any claim like "spot fluid overload early," "helps control your blood pressure," or "know when to call your nephrologist" destroys it immediately.
3. Tighten the intended purpose with explicit limitations: not for diagnosis, not for acute or urgent decisions, no alarms or notifications, not a substitute for clinical measurement, output must be interpreted by a qualified clinician alongside other clinical data. Put these in the IFU and in-app.
4. **Get a national competent authority or notified body view before launch.** This is a well-known borderline case and practice varies between member states; a €5k opinion now is cheaper than a reclassification later.

One flag worth stating plainly: in my experience of how these are assessed post-MDR, apps of exactly this shape usually end up as IIa. If your business plan depends on being out of scope, stress-test that assumption early rather than building to it.

I'm not a regulatory consultant and this isn't a formal regulatory opinion — treat it as a starting analysis to take to one.

## Short answer

Two-step question, and the first step matters more than the class.

**Step 1 — is it a medical device at all?** As described, you have a genuinely defensible argument that it is **not** MDSW, i.e. outside MDR entirely.

**Step 2 — if it is a device, it's Class IIa** under Annex VIII Rule 11. There is no realistic path to Class I here.

## Why it may not be a device

MDCG 2019-11's decision tree fails the product out at Step 3: is the software *performing an action on data beyond storage, archival, communication, simple search, or lossless compression?*

Your app stores patient-entered numbers and draws them on a time axis. Plotting stored values is display, not computation on the data — no interpretation, no thresholds, no normal/abnormal classification, no risk score, no prediction. That's the classic "patient diary / simple record-keeping" pattern that MDCG 2019-11 and MHRA guidance both treat as non-device. The absence of alarms and of any acute use supports this.

The counter-argument a competent authority could make: CKD is a disease, weight and BP trends are exactly how fluid status and hypertension are managed, and a nephrologist reading that chart is *monitoring* the disease — which is a medical purpose under Art. 2(1). This is a real borderline, not a slam dunk, and different national authorities have gone different ways on near-identical apps.

## If it is a device: Rule 11 → Class IIa

Rule 11 first limb: *software intended to provide information used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes* → **Class IIa**.

- Not **III**: the decisions it informs (diuretic dose, antihypertensive adjustment at a scheduled visit) don't cause death or irreversible deterioration if the trend is wrong.
- Not **IIb**: no surgical intervention, no serious deterioration on the immediate path. Under the second limb, BP is a vital physiological parameter, but once-daily home readings reviewed weeks later are not variations "of such a nature that they could result in immediate danger" — that limb targets continuous/acute monitoring.
- Not **I**: the "all other software is Class I" fallback is nearly dead in practice. MDCG 2019-11 is explicit that it applies only where the software drives no clinical decision at all — and if you've already conceded the software is MDSW because a nephrologist uses it clinically, you've conceded the first limb of Rule 11.

That asymmetry is the whole commercial story: **non-device → nothing; device → IIa with a notified body, ISO 13485 QMS, Annex IX/XI conformity assessment, clinical evaluation, PMS/PMCF, UDI, EUDAMED.** There is no cheap middle.

## What decides it

Things that keep you outside MDR:
- Intended-purpose statement stays exactly as narrow as you've written it — and marketing matches it. Claims are what regulators read first.
- No colour-coded ranges, no "high/low/normal" labels, no target lines, no trend arrows with interpretation.
- No alerts, notifications, or "contact your doctor" triggers.
- No fitted trend lines, projections, or derived metrics (e.g. dry-weight estimates, rate-of-gain per week).
- Presented as a record the patient keeps and shows, not as a clinical tool.

Things that flip it to IIa immediately: any threshold or alarm, any interpretation of the trend, any dosing or fluid-restriction guidance, any prediction, or connecting a BP cuff *and* claiming clinical monitoring on top of it. (Note: pairing with a cuff alone is a data-source question, but it usually comes with monitoring claims that do the damage.)

Write the qualification rationale as a formal document now — the MDCG 2019-11 decision steps, your answer at each, and the evidence — and keep it under change control alongside the marketing copy. Then get it confirmed: a borderline determination from your competent authority (or a written notified-body opinion) is cheap relative to discovering at launch that you're an unregistered IIa. Even as a non-device you still have GDPR/special-category data obligations, and if you're targeting Germany's DiGA route or similar reimbursement schemes, those *require* device status — which would make Class IIa a deliberate goal rather than a risk.

I'd be reasonably confident in the non-device position as written, but I'd want it on paper and confirmed rather than assumed. This is my read of the regulation, not regulatory advice.

Weight and BP in CKD are proxies for fluid overload and hypertension control — this is monitoring of a disease.
- **The output feeds a therapeutic decision.** The nephrologist looks at the trend and adjusts dry weight target, diuretics, antihypertensives. That's the Rule 11 first limb almost verbatim.

The one thing that could keep it out is **MDCG 2019-11 decision step 3**: does the software perform an action on data *beyond* storage, archival, communication, simple search or lossless compression? If not, it isn't MDSW. MDCG also notes that altering the *representation* of data for cosmetic/compatibility reasons isn't an action on data.

So: **a plain line chart of exactly what the patient typed, with a date axis, is arguably display, not computation.** A pure electronic diary. But the word "trends" is doing a lot of work in your description. If the app computes rolling averages, week-over-week deltas, a regression/trend line, "% change since last visit", or highlights readings against any threshold — that is derived medical information about an identifiable patient, and you are MDSW.

**Draw that line explicitly in your requirements, and write it into the IFU.** It is the whole decision.

## Step 2 — If it is a device: Rule 11 → Class IIa

- **Not Class I.** "All other software" only catches software that neither informs diagnostic/therapeutic decisions nor monitors physiological processes. You do both. Competent authorities have consistently rejected the Class I reading for clinical apps post-MDR; the MDD Class I self-certification route for this kind of product is gone.
- **Not Class IIb.** BP *is* a vital physiological parameter, so the second limb's IIb exception is live in principle — but it requires that variations "could result in immediate danger." No alarms, no acute use, review weeks later at a scheduled appointment: that's a clean argument against immediate danger. Document it in your classification rationale rather than leaving it implied.
- **Not Class III.** No plausible death/irreversible-deterioration pathway from a retrospective trend chart.

So IIa, via either limb.

Notified body involvement, ISO 13485 QMS, IEC 62304 (likely software safety Class A given no alarms and no acute use — argue this early, it saves a lot), ISO 14971, IEC 62366-1, IEC 82304-1 for standalone health software, clinical evaluation under Annex XIV (a literature route is plausible here, probably no clinical investigation), UDI, PMS/PMCF, Annex XI or Annex IX conformity assessment. Realistically 12–24 months and a six-figure budget. Materially different product plan from a non-device diary.

## Recommendation

Decide deliberately which product you're building rather than discovering it at audit:

1. **Non-device diary.** Restrict the app to storing and plotting raw entered values, verbatim, no derived statistics, no thresholds, no interpretation. Reword the intended purpose to drop "trend": *"to allow patients to record their own weight and blood pressure measurements and to display those recorded values, for their own reference and to show to a healthcare professional."* Remove the disease naming from the intended purpose if the app genuinely isn't CKD-specific. Then write a formal qualification rationale against MDCG 2019-11 and keep it. This is defensible, but it is a thin margin — any future "your average is trending up" feature crosses the line.
2. **Accept IIa and build for it.** If the trending analysis is the actual value proposition (and for CKD fluid management, it probably is), fighting for non-device status will hobble the product and leave you exposed. Better to scope for IIa now.

## Short answer

**Class I**, under Rule 11's residual limb ("all other software"), with Rule 11 first paragraph (Class IIa) being the argument you have to be ready to rebut.

One flag before the reasoning: the stated function — reformat and route a finalised, signed report without altering content — is close to the textbook example of software that *doesn't* qualify as MDSW at all under MDCG 2019-11, which excludes action limited to "storage, archival, communication, simple search [or] lossless compression." You've said qualification is settled, so I'll take it as given, but the same logic that makes qualification shaky is what drives the classification answer below.

## Route through Annex VIII

- **Implementing rule 3.3 (Chapter II):** software that drives or influences another device takes that device's class; software independent of any other device is classified in its own right. This is independent of the modality/PACS — it neither drives nor influences them — so it's classified on its own.
- **Rule 11 (Chapter III)** is then the only substantive rule that bites. Rules 1–10 and 12–22 are about invasiveness, active therapeutic/diagnostic devices with energy, substances, etc. Rule 11 has three limbs:
  1. software providing information used to take decisions with diagnostic or therapeutic purposes → **IIa**, escalating to IIb (serious deterioration / surgical intervention) or III (death / irreversible deterioration);
  2. software intended to monitor physiological processes → IIa, or IIb for vital parameters with immediate-danger variation;
  3. **all other software → Class I.**
- Limb 2 plainly doesn't apply. So the whole question is limb 1 vs limb 3.

## Why limb 1 doesn't apply

The decisive words are "**provide information**." Under MDCG 2019-11, the information contemplated by Rule 11 is information the software itself creates or derives — through calculation, analysis, interpretation, or combination of data. Here:

- the diagnostic information is authored and signed by the radiologist *before* the software touches it;
- the software's action is presentational and logistical — re-laying-out and delivering an unchanged clinical payload;
- it contributes no new clinical content, no derived value, no prioritisation, no interpretation. Remove the software and the GP gets the identical clinical information by another route.

A conduit for someone else's decision-support output is not itself providing information for a decision within the meaning of Rule 11 — otherwise every e-mail gateway, DICOM router and hospital messaging bus carrying a report would be Class IIa, which is not how Rule 11 is applied. So limb 3 applies: **Class I**.

## The counter-argument, and where it actually has teeth

A notified body or competent authority may push a literal reading: the GP demonstrably uses that report to make diagnostic and therapeutic decisions, the software is what puts it in front of them, therefore IIa. This literalism is well documented as Rule 11's central drafting problem. Your defence is the create-vs-transmit distinction above, and it should hold — **provided** the intended purpose and the actual behaviour stay clean. It collapses if the software does any of:

- selecting, summarising, truncating, or reordering content by clinical significance;
- flagging, highlighting, or triaging urgent findings;
- routing based on clinical content rather than administrative identifiers (referrer, episode, order number);
- lossy transformation of embedded measurements, tables, or key images.

Any of those turn presentation into derivation and take you to IIa (and would settle the qualification question against you at the same time). Your stated intended purpose — "to reformat and route finalised radiology reports to referring physicians" — is well drafted for the Class I position: it is deliberately administrative and content-neutral. Keep it that way in the IFU, labelling and marketing claims, because classification follows intended purpose, and marketing copy about "making sure clinicians never miss a critical result" would do real damage.

Note also that failure modes — mangled layout, misrouted report, silent non-delivery causing a missed follow-up — are genuine and belong squarely in your ISO 14971 risk file and your Annex I GSPR 17 software-lifecycle evidence. They do **not** raise the class: Annex VIII classification runs on intended purpose, not on hazard severity of malfunction.

## Practical consequences of Class I

Self-certification: no notified body for conformity assessment. You still owe the full Annex II/III technical documentation, GSPR conformity (notably GSPR 17 on programmable systems, plus IEC 62304 as state of the art), a QMS meeting Article 10(9), clinical evaluation under Article 61 and Annex XIV, PMS under Articles 83–86, a Declaration of Conformity, UDI assignment, CE marking without a notified-body number, Actor/device registration in EUDAMED, and a PRRC. Not sterile, not measuring, not reusable surgical — so none of the Class I NB-involvement carve-outs in Article 52(7) apply.

If you need this to survive audit, the single most valuable artefact is a short classification rationale memo recording the Rule 11 limb-1-vs-limb-3 analysis explicitly, rather than just asserting Class I — reviewers challenge silent Rule 11 conclusions far more often than reasoned ones.

*(If Great Britain is also in scope, UK MDR 2002 still runs the pre-MDR rules, where standalone software of this type sits in Class I under the old Rule 12 — same outcome, different reasoning. Switzerland mirrors MDR.)*

## Class I

Rule 11 is the applicable rule (Annex VIII, Chapter III, section 6.3), and this software lands in its residual limb:

> "Software intended to provide information which is used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes is class IIa… Software intended to monitor physiological processes is class IIa… **All other software is classified as class I.**"

**Why not IIa:** Rule 11's first indent requires the software itself to *provide information* that feeds a diagnostic or therapeutic decision. Here the diagnostic information is created and signed by the clinician; your software adds no data, derives nothing, does not analyse, prioritise, flag, or triage. It moves and re-lays-out an already-final human decision. Per MDCG 2019-11, pure communication/transmission/storage functions with no alteration of clinical content sit outside the "provides information for decisions" limb, so the residual sentence applies. The IIb/III escalations are irrelevant because they only qualify the first indent — you never enter it.

Also relevant to confirm nothing else bites:
- **Implementing rule 3.3** — it's standalone, not driving or influencing a hardware device, so it is classified in its own right rather than inheriting a parent device's class.
- **Implementing rule 3.5** (highest applicable class) — no other rule applies; Rule 11 is the software rule and outranks Rule 13's generic "all other active devices are class I" landing spot, though both give the same result.
- Not Class Is / Im / Ir / Is-sup — no sterility, no measuring function, not reusable surgical, not a substance-based device. So it's **plain Class I: self-certification, no notified body.**

**Two things worth flagging**

1. **The stipulated qualification is doing a lot of work.** MDCG 2019-11 treats software that only changes layout/format for compatibility or presentation purposes, without altering clinical content, as *not* qualifying as MDSW at all. Your description matches that exclusion almost exactly. Taking qualification as given, Class I is the answer — but if that premise came from an internal decision rather than a competent-authority position, it's the part most likely to be challenged, in the direction of "not a device."

2. **The intended purpose is what holds Class I in place, and it's fragile.** "Reformat and route finalised reports" is safely residual. Class I evaporates the moment the product does any of: highlighting or extracting critical findings, sorting/prioritising the GP inbox by urgency, summarising the report, generating alerts for unread critical results, or applying rules that suppress or reorder clinical content. Each of those pulls you into Rule 11's first indent at **IIa** or higher — and inbox-triage-by-urgency features are a common creep path. Keep the IFU, marketing claims, and backlog aligned to the narrow wording.

**Class I obligations still apply in full:** Annex II/III technical documentation, GSPR conformity assessment against Annex I (including Annex I §17 software requirements — verification, validation, IT security, and the mobile/host-platform provisions), IEC 62304-style lifecycle evidence, Annex XIV clinical evaluation, Article 10(9) QMS (ISO 13485 in practice), risk management to ISO 14971, Basic UDI-DI and UDI assignment, EUDAMED/competent-authority registration, Article 19 Declaration of Conformity signed under your own responsibility, CE mark, and Articles 83–86 PMS with a PMS report. Note that misrouting to the wrong GP is both a safety and a GDPR issue, so your risk file and cybersecurity documentation should address routing integrity and delivery confirmation explicitly, even at Class I.

## Class I — Rule 11, final limb

**Applicable rule:** Annex VIII, Chapter III, Section 6.3 (Rule 11) is the rule for software. Since the software is standalone, implementing rule 3.3 sends it to be "classified in its own right" rather than inheriting the class of any hardware device.

**Working through Rule 11's limbs:**

| Limb | Applies? |
|---|---|
| Provides information used to take decisions with diagnostic/therapeutic purposes → IIa (III if death/irreversible deterioration; IIb if serious deterioration or surgical intervention) | No — on the stated facts the software creates no new information and modifies none. The diagnostic information was created and signed by the clinician; the software changes only its presentation and destination. |
| Intended to monitor physiological processes → IIa (IIb for vital parameters with immediate danger) | No |
| **All other software → Class I** | **Yes** |

Implementing rule 3.5 (highest applicable rule wins) doesn't bite, since no higher limb is triggered.

## The pressure point

The friction here isn't classification, it's the premise. MDCG 2019-11 says software intended only to store, archive, communicate, losslessly compress, or perform simple search is *not* medical device software. Reformat-and-route is squarely in that description, so the natural answer is "not a device at all." You've stipulated qualification, so I've taken it as given — but it's worth knowing *why* it was qualified, because the reason usually reveals whether the "adds nothing, alters nothing" description fully holds:

- If reformatting involves any restructuring that could change what the GP reads first, drop content, truncate, or reorder findings versus impression — that starts to look like altering the representation of clinical data, and a notified body could argue the first limb of Rule 11 applies, giving **Class IIa**. That's the realistic worst case, not IIb/III.
- If it was qualified because routing errors have patient-safety consequences (report to the wrong GP, or silently not delivered), that's a risk-management concern, not a Rule 11 trigger. Rule 11 classifies on intended purpose, not on failure severity. Class I stands.

## What Class I actually means here

Not "nothing to do" — it's self-declaration, but with the full obligation set:

- No notified body (Article 52(7) — it's not sterile, measuring, or reusable surgical)
- QMS under Article 10(9); technical documentation per Annexes II and III
- Clinical evaluation under Article 61 and Annex XIV (proportionate, but required)
- Annex I Section 17 for programmable electronic systems — IEC 62304 and IEC 82304-1 are the expected state of the art
- UDI, EUDAMED registration, PMS plan and PMS report

One other thing to check: if the hospital both develops and uses this internally and doesn't transfer it to another legal entity, **Article 5(5)** (health institution exemption) may apply, which changes the compliance path substantially. "Standalone software used in hospitals" leaves that ambiguous, and it's the difference between a full Class I conformity route and the in-house derogation.

## Short answer: I can't give you a class, and the reason matters for marketing

Classification presumes qualification. Annex VIII tells you *which class* a medical device is; it doesn't tell you *whether* you have a medical device. That's Art. 2(1), which is a separate analysis this skill doesn't cover — and on your description, nothing establishes that your app is a device at all.

A habit tracker that logs water, steps and sleep, returns a wellness score and sends encouragement, with no medical claims, is on its face a wellness product outside MDR scope. Products outside the scope of MDR do not have an MDR class. Not class I — *no class*.

## Why this is the answer marketing actually needs

**Putting a class on the website would be a regulatory claim about the product.** Saying "MDR Class I" asserts that you are a medical device — self-certified, with a technical file, a QMS, clinical evaluation, post-market surveillance, UDI, a Declaration of Conformity, and an EU registration. If you say it and don't have those, you've claimed device status you can't support. If you genuinely aren't a device, the accurate statement is that MDR doesn't apply.

So the useful thing to hand marketing is not a class. It's either:

- "Not a medical device — this app is intended for general wellness and fitness and makes no medical claims," or
- nothing at all about MDR.

That second one is usually the safer default, because a *negative* claim still invites the question.

## What I'd need to classify, if you do want the exercise run

1. **The intended purpose as written in your technical documentation** — verbatim, not a paraphrase. Implementing rule 3.1 anchors classification to the stated intended purpose, not to what the software can do `[verified]`.
2. **A settled qualification determination** — that Art. 2(1) is met `[verify]`.

## The part that should give you some pause

Two things in your description are where wellness apps drift into scope, and they're worth checking before marketing writes anything:

**The wellness score.** If the score is ever presented as telling a user something about their *health state* — a risk indicator, a "your sleep is unhealthy" reading, anything a user would reasonably act on — you're closer to limb 2 of Rule 11, "software intended to monitor physiological processes," base class **IIa** `[verified]`. Sleep and hydration are physiological. The thing keeping you out isn't the data type, it's the intended purpose. Note that the IIb escalation on that limb needs *both* vital parameters *and* variation that could cause immediate danger `[verified]` — neither applies here.

**The encouragement messages.** If any message advises a user to change behaviour on health grounds, or reacts to logged values ("your intake is low, drink more"), someone will ask whether that's information used to take a therapeutic decision — limb 1, base class **IIa** `[verified]`.

I raise these because 3.1 cuts both ways: it protects you from being classified on capability alone, but it also means a marketing page that describes the app in health terms can become evidence about your intended purpose. **The website copy is a regulatory artifact.** If the site says "improve your health" and the technical file says "general wellness," the mismatch is the exposure — and it's exactly the kind of thing that gets found later. Whatever marketing publishes should match the intended purpose in your documentation word for word.

One more: if the app takes in data from a connected wearable or scale rather than only manual logging, implementing rule 3.3 comes into play — software that drives a device or influences its use takes that device's class `[verified]`. ## Bottom line: Class IIa, MDR Annex VIII Rule 11, first indent

Not Class I. The framing you've given ("it's the treatment, it doesn't feed information to anyone to decide anything") is exactly the argument that gets a Class I self-declaration challenged, and I'd advise against building your route on it.

## Why Rule 11's first indent bites

Rule 11 first indent: *software intended to provide information which is used to take decisions with diagnosis or therapeutic purposes* → IIa (higher tiers by harm severity).

MDCG 2019-11 is explicit that "decisions" are not limited to clinician decisions — the decision-taker may be a healthcare professional, **the patient, or a lay user**. Removing the clinician from the loop doesn't remove the decision; it relocates it to the patient. MDCG 2021-24 reiterates the same reading for Rule 11.

Your programme unavoidably outputs patient-actionable therapeutic instructions:

- **Sleep restriction scheduling** — "your prescribed sleep window is 00:45–05:45" is a computed, individualised, therapeutic instruction that the patient acts on nightly, and that the software titrates from their diary data. This is the strongest single fact against Class I.
- **Stimulus control** — "leave the bed if awake >20 minutes."
- **Cognitive restructuring** — arguably more educational, and weaker on its own, but it doesn't rescue the package.

The "software *is* the therapy, so it isn't *informing* a decision" argument is a genuine reading of the literal text — Rule 11 was drafted around information-provision and monitoring, and pure therapy-delivery software sits in a recognised gap. But it's a minority position that notified bodies and competent authorities have consistently declined to accept for DTx, and it's the position that produced the whole Rule 11 up-classification wave (the reason so many Class I legacy software devices needed the extended MDR transition provisions with notified-body involvement). Betting a market launch on it means a self-certified Class I device that a competent authority can force off the market.

## The IIa vs IIb question is the one actually worth your attention

Rule 11 escalates to IIb where the decision may cause serious deterioration of health, and III where death or irreversible deterioration. For CBT-I the specific hazards are real and well documented:

- Sleep restriction can precipitate **mania or hypomania** in bipolar disorder.
- Sleep restriction can **lower the seizure threshold** in epilepsy.
- Induced daytime sleepiness → **driving and occupational-machinery risk**, especially in weeks 2–3.
- Masking **undiagnosed OSA** or another organic cause by treating the presenting complaint.

IIa is defensible, but only if your contraindication screening, exclusion criteria, driving/machinery warnings and escalation-to-clinician pathways are strong and evidenced in the risk file. If screening is weak or advisory-only, expect a notified body to push toward IIb. I'd design the screening gate as a hard, non-skippable enrolment control specifically so IIa holds.

## Rules you can dismiss, with reasons on record

- **Rule 22** (active therapeutic device with integrated diagnostic function significantly determining patient management → III): the diary-driven titration is a feedback loop, but there's no diagnostic function in the closed-loop/AED sense. Dismissable — but document the reasoning, because it does get raised for adaptive DTx.
- **Rule 11 second indent** (monitoring physiological processes → IIa; vital parameters with immediate danger → IIb): doesn't apply to patient-entered sleep diaries. **It does apply if you ingest actigraphy or wearable sleep data** — that lands you at IIa via a second route, still not IIb, since sleep parameters aren't vital parameters where variation causes immediate danger. If a wearable is in scope, say so and I'll rework this.
- **Rules 9/10**: no energy administered or exchanged; not applicable to standalone software here.
- Annex VIII implementing rule 3.5: where several rules apply, the highest class governs.

## Practical consequences

- Notified body required. Annex IX (QMS + technical documentation assessment, with the Chapter III surveillance) is the usual route; Annex XI Part A is available for IIa but rarely chosen for software.
- ISO 14971, IEC 62304 (software safety class likely B, C if you accept the mania/seizure pathway as death-or-serious-injury-capable), IEC 62366-1, and clinical evaluation under Annex XIV. For a IIa DTx making a treatment claim, expect to need your own clinical investigation data, not just literature on face-to-face CBT-I — equivalence to in-person therapy is not a route a notified body will accept.
- If Germany is a target market, DiGA now accommodates up to risk class IIb following the Digital Act, so IIa is no obstacle to fast-track listing.

## Suggested wording for the technical documentation

> Classified as Class IIa under Rule 11, first indent, Annex VIII of Regulation (EU) 2017/745. The device provides individualised therapeutic instructions (sleep window prescription, stimulus control rules) that are used by the patient to take decisions with a therapeutic purpose. Consistent with MDCG 2019-11, the decision-taker for the purposes of Rule 11 is the patient. The decisions concerned are not capable of causing death or irreversible deterioration of health, and — given the mandatory contraindication screening and use restrictions specified in [ref] — are not capable of causing serious deterioration of health or necessitating surgical intervention; Class IIb and Class III are therefore not applicable.

## Bottom line

**Class I, via Rule 11's residual limb** ("all other software is classified as class I") — but this is the single most contested corner of Rule 11, and I'd document the reasoning defensively because a competent authority or notified body could push you to IIa.

## Rule 11 walk-through (Annex VIII, MDR 2017/745)

**Limb 1 — information for decisions → IIa/IIb/III.** This requires the software to *provide information which is used to take decisions* with diagnostic or therapeutic purposes. Your product doesn't inform a decision made downstream by someone else; it *is* the therapeutic intervention. The intended purpose is to treat, not to inform. On your facts (no clinician in the loop, no output feeding anyone's decision), limb 1 doesn't bite.

The counter-argument you should expect: MDCG 2019-11 confirms the "decision" can be taken by the **patient**, not only an HCP. A CBT-I programme outputs a personalised sleep window and stimulus-control instructions the patient then acts on. A reviewer can characterise that as information used by the patient to take therapeutic decisions → **IIa**. This reading is why several DTx have been up-classified. It's a live disagreement across member states, not a settled point.

**Limb 2 — monitoring physiological processes → IIa/IIb.** Self-reported sleep diaries aren't device monitoring of a physiological process. If you integrate actigraphy/wearable-derived sleep data *within the intended purpose*, limb 2 becomes arguable → IIa.

**Limb 3 — residual → Class I.** Where you land.

**Other rules checked:** implementing rule 3.3 (software independent of any other device is classified in its own right — applies, it's standalone); 3.5 (highest applicable class wins, if a second rule is triggered); Rule 22 doesn't apply (no active therapeutic device with integrated diagnostic function in the hardware sense). Prescription-only status is irrelevant to MDR classification — that's a US framing.

## What flips this to IIa — check each before you commit

1. **Screening or eligibility logic.** If onboarding scores an instrument (ISI, sleep apnoea screener, depression/suicidality items) and routes the user — "you may not be suitable, see your doctor" — that's information for a decision. This is the most common trap; most DTx have it.
2. **Safety-netting / escalation flags** during the programme (deterioration, suicidal ideation alerts).
3. **Any clinician-facing dashboard or report**, even optional or post-programme.
4. **Wearable/actigraphy integration** in the intended purpose (limb 2).
5. **Claims framing.** If marketing or the IFU describes the output as "personalised recommendations" or "guidance," you've argued yourself into limb 1.

If any of 1–4 is in scope, classify **IIa** and take the notified body route. Nothing here plausibly reaches IIb/III — sleep restriction causes daytime sleepiness (a real driving-safety issue for your risk file and IFU warnings), but that's not "serious deterioration of health or a surgical intervention."

## If Class I holds

Self-declaration under Art. 52(7) — no notified body. But everything else still applies in full: Annex I GSPRs, Annex II/III technical documentation, QMS under Art. 10(9) (ISO 13485 in practice), IEC 62304 + 82304-1, ISO 14971, PMS/PMCF plan, UDI, EUDAMED and Art. 31 registration, PRRC.

Clinical evaluation is your real cost driver, not the class. A hard treatment claim for chronic insomnia won't survive Art. 61/Annex XIV on literature and equivalence alone — plan an RCT. That also serves German DiGA listing (open to Class I and IIa), if that's your market entry.

## Practical advice

Write the classification rationale into the technical documentation as an explicit Rule 11 analysis that *names* the limb-1 patient-decision argument and rebuts it, rather than silently asserting Class I. If you're going to a DiGA/BfArM or national CA interaction, pre-align there. Re-check MDCG 2019-11 and MDCG 2021-24 for the current revision before filing — this area has been moving.

## Short answer

**Class IIa, under Annex VIII Rule 11, first indent.**

The "it's the therapy, not information for a decision" argument is the right argument to *make*, but it isn't the one that wins, and I'd plan on IIa rather than build a regulatory strategy around Class I.

## Why Rule 11 first indent still catches you

Two of the framings in your brief don't do the work you want them to:

**"No clinician in the loop."** Rule 11 doesn't care who takes the decision. MDCG 2019-11 is explicit that the decision-maker can be a healthcare professional, the patient, or a lay person. Removing the clinician removes a mitigation, if anything — it doesn't remove the device from the rule.

**"It doesn't feed information to anyone to decide anything."** Sleep restriction scheduling does exactly this. The software ingests diary data, computes a personalised sleep window, and outputs "your bed time is 00:45, your rise time is 06:15." The patient then acts on it. That is information with a therapeutic purpose that a person uses to take a decision — under the plain wording of the rule and under MDCG 2019-11's reading of it. Stimulus control instructions and cognitive restructuring prompts are weaker cases individually, but the sleep window alone is enough to pull the device in.

The third indent ("all other software" → Class I) is understood as a residual bucket for software that doesn't act on the clinical pathway: viewers, storage and archiving, lossless compression, communication, simple search. A device whose intended purpose contains the verb "treat" is a very hard fit for it. Post-MDR, this is precisely where the mass up-classification of standalone health software happened, and notified bodies have been consistently unreceptive to the "delivery, not decision support" distinction.

## Why not higher

The IIb escalation asks whether the decisions could cause serious deterioration of health. There's a real argument to rebut here, and your notified body will raise it:

- Sleep restriction deliberately induces acute sleep deprivation — drowsy driving and occupational accident risk
- Sleep deprivation can precipitate mania in undiagnosed bipolar disorder and lower the seizure threshold in epilepsy
- An unsupervised programme may mask undiagnosed obstructive sleep apnoea

The counter, which I think holds: harm doesn't follow from a single erroneous output but from sustained adherence over weeks, with in-programme feedback and titration; the patient retains control at every step; and the high-risk populations are excluded by screening and contraindications. **Land at IIa, but write that rationale into your classification justification rather than leaving the NB to find the question themselves.** Class III is not in play — nothing here plausibly causes death or irreversible deterioration.

## What this actually costs you

- **Notified body involvement** — Annex IX Chapters I + III (QMS plus technical documentation assessment on a sampling basis), or Annex XI Part A. This is the main delta from Class I and the main schedule driver.
- **ISO 13485 QMS**, certified.
- **Clinical evidence.** A "treat chronic insomnia" claim needs data demonstrating that treatment effect. Equivalence routes under Article 61 are difficult for software — you generally can't get the technical and biological equivalence you need against another CBT-I product. Assume your own clinical investigation. See MDCG 2020-1 on clinical evaluation of MDSW.
- **Standards:** IEC 62304, ISO 14971, IEC 62366-1, IEC 82304-1.
- **PMCF plan and PSUR** obligations.

One thing people routinely conflate: your **IEC 62304 software safety class is a separate axis** from the MDR class. Given the harm scenarios above, expect to justify Class B, and be ready for a challenge toward C if you can't argue that the accident/mania pathways are non-serious after external risk controls.

## Two things I'd tighten

**Sharpen the intended purpose.** "To treat chronic insomnia in adults by delivering CBT-I" is doing a lot of load-bearing work — it drives classification, the clinical evidence burden, and the scope of your claims. Bound it explicitly: adults 18+ with chronic insomnia disorder per DSM-5/ICSD-3, with stated exclusions for untreated OSA, bipolar disorder, seizure disorders, and safety-critical occupations. Those exclusions are simultaneously your risk controls and your defence against the IIb argument.

**Check whether you have a legacy position.** If this product held an MDD Class I declaration of conformity drawn up before 26 May 2021, the Regulation 2023/607 transitional provisions could have applied — but the gating deadlines (MDR QMS and formal NB application by 26 May 2024, signed agreement by 26 September 2024) are well past as of today. If you didn't meet them, that route is closed and you're on a straight MDR IIa conformity assessment. If this is a new product, it was never available anyway.

Worth saying plainly: classification is formally yours to determine and your notified body's to accept, and a competent authority can disagree with both. But on the facts as you've given them, IIa is where I'd expect this to sit, and I'd not spend cycles pursuing Class I.

Short answer: on what you've described, the question isn't classification — it's **qualification**, and that's a different analysis from the one Annex VIII settles.

## The two questions, kept apart

**Is it MDSW?** That runs on Art. 2(1) MDR (the device definition), not Annex VIII. Nothing in the classification rules answers it, and I shouldn't classify a hospital document-retrieval tool just because the question arrived in classification terms. If it doesn't qualify, there is no class and no Rule 11 analysis to do.

**If it did qualify**, the Annex VIII route would be: 3.3 — independent software, not driving or influencing another device → classified in its own right → Rule 11. Pure retrieval with no interpretation doesn't engage limb 1 (information used to take diagnostic/therapeutic decisions) or limb 2 (monitoring physiological processes), so it would land in limb 3, **class I**. `[verified]` — Rule 11 and 3.3 are verbatim from EUR-Lex, CELEX 32017R0745, retrieved 2026-09-09.

But that's the conditional. The real answer to your question is upstream.

## The "simple search" authority — and its status

The simple-search / adds-value distinction **is not in the MDR**. It appears nowhere in Annex VIII or the articles. It comes from **MDCG 2019-11**, *Guidance on Qualification and Classification of Software in Regulation (EU) 2017/745 – MDR and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 – IVDR*, in the decision-steps section on whether software "processes, analyses, creates or modifies medical information."

The shape of it, as I recall it: software that processes, analyses, creates or modifies medical information may be MDSW where that is governed by a medical intended purpose — and *simple search*, meaning retrieval of records by matching record metadata against search criteria, is expressly carved out as not amounting to that.

Two cautions on this:

1. **MDCG 2019-11 is Commission guidance, not the regulation.** It has no binding force. It's persuasive with notified bodies and it's what your reviewer will likely reach for, but it is not authority in the sense the MDR text is.
2. **I could not verify the passage.** I tried to fetch MDCG 2019-11 to quote you the exact wording and section number, and web access was denied in this session. So treat my paraphrase above as recalled, not checked. `[verify]` — don't put it in a technical file or a notified-body submission on my say-so. If you re-enable web access I'll pull the actual text and give you the section and the verbatim sentence.

## What would flip your tool into qualifying

The carve-out is narrower than "we don't rank." Worth testing your intended purpose against each of these:

- Matching against **patient-specific data** rather than a document query — that's the classic tipping point in the guidance.
- **Relevance ranking on clinical criteria**, which you've excluded — good, but confirm nothing in the roadmap reintroduces it.
- **Filtering that is itself a clinical judgment** (e.g. "only guidelines applicable to this patient's condition").
- **Summarising, extracting, or restructuring** content from the retrieved documents.

Write the intended purpose down now, in the negative as well as the positive — "retrieval of existing documents by metadata match; does not rank by clinical relevance, does not interpret, does not select for a specific patient" — and make that statement the thing product changes get tested against. **MDCG 2019-11**, *Guidance on Qualification and Classification of Software in Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR) and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (IVDR)*. Issued by the Medical Device Coordination Group (the Art. 103 MDR body — Commission plus member state competent authorities). This is defined in a footnote to that step, and it is the exact line you're asking about:

> "Simple search" refers to the retrieval of records by matching record metadata against record search criteria, e.g. library functions. Simple search does not cover software which provides interpretative search results, e.g. to identify medical findings in health records or based on patient's health data.

So the official dividing line is **interpretation, not value**. A search tool can be enormously valuable, fast, and well-designed and still be non-device. What pulls it across is generating something that wasn't in the library — a judgment about clinical meaning or patient-specific applicability.

The guidance reinforces this elsewhere: Hospital Information Systems and EHR-type products that store and retrieve without acting on the data are given as non-device examples.

Any of these, and you're arguing uphill:

- Ranking or scoring results by **clinical** relevance (you've correctly excluded this — note that ranking by recency, document type, or department is not clinical and is fine)
- Filtering or ordering against **patient data** — "documents relevant to this patient" is interpretative
- Snippet generation, summarisation, or any LLM answer layer over the retrieved documents
- Flagging, highlighting, or surfacing findings within documents

And the one teams miss: **intended purpose is set by what the manufacturer claims**, not by the architecture (MDR Art. 2(12)). A sales deck or UI string saying "finds the right protocol for your patient" can create a medical claim your code doesn't make. Lock the intended purpose statement and police the marketing copy against it.

Worth knowing the stakes: if it did qualify, Rule 11 (MDR Annex VIII) puts information-providing software at **Class IIa minimum**, with higher classes where decisions could cause serious deterioration or death. That's a notified body and a full QMS. Which is why this line is worth documenting properly rather than assuming.

**Grey zone to be aware of:** the footnote describes matching *metadata* against search criteria. Keyword/BM25 retrieval is squarely inside. Embedding-based semantic retrieval is not addressed by any official position I'm aware of — the defensible argument is that it's still pure retrieval because no new information is created, but if you're using vector search, know that you're reasoning by analogy rather than citing a settled rule.

**US (FDA):** same principle, different words. Write a short qualification rationale memo — one page — that cites MDCG 2019-11 Step 3 and the simple-search footnote, states the intended purpose verbatim, and lists the excluded functions (no scoring, no ranking, no interpretation).
